title: Eshrahli
summary: Upload your lecture slides and get them explained in Arabic with the English technical terms left intact — so the concept lands in your own language and the exam vocabulary comes with it.
body:
## The problem

Students at UDST who did their secondary education in Arabic-medium government schools sit through lectures delivered in English. The gap is not vocabulary at the surface — it is the distance between recognising an English word and understanding the concept behind it well enough to be examined on it.

Translating the material outright does not fix that. It removes the English terms the exam will actually use.

## What we built

Eshrahli takes a student's own lecture slides — PDF or PPTX, organised into course folders — and explains each slide in flowing Arabic with every key English technical term left in English and bolded inline. The student follows the concept in their own language and absorbs the terminology they will be assessed on at the same time.

The bilingual spine is the design decision, not a feature. In the beta it was the thing students asked us not to remove.

Behind it is a retrieval pipeline in four steps: parse and chunk the course PDF; enrich figures and equations with vision so diagrams are readable rather than skipped; retrieve against the student's question; and generate with a RISEN-structured prompt — role, instruction, steps, end goal, narrowing — that instructs the model to teach rather than summarise.

Every answer is grounded in the student's own upload. There is no drift onto a different syllabus, and where retrieval is not confident enough the system refuses rather than guessing. Answers carry page-level citations.

## Security

The sprint asked for a security assessment, and three risks drove real changes rather than a document.

Prompt injection is handled by a defensive block at the top of the system prompt that refuses attempts to override the role, reveal instructions, or answer off-topic — and by a post-generation validator between the model and the screen that replaces off-scope output with a safe fallback before a student sees it. Two layers, because a prompt alone is not a control.

Access is scoped by authentication: every folder, slide and saved explanation is stored under a user ID, and every database query and retrieval is filtered to the signed-in student. Uploaded coursework is private.

## Where it stands

An end-to-end MVP, deployed, with course folders, vision-enriched ingestion, slide-level explanations, follow-up Q&A and generated quizzes. It has been through a qualitative beta with UDST students on their own coursework.

The plan is a paid launch at UDST for the spring semester — students first, and a campus licence only once that has proved demand.

## My role

Co-founder and CEO. Built with Khaled Mhirsi, co-founder and CTO, for the UHUB × Scale AI Sprint, where it won the general track.

title: Rubric
summary: One shared pool of applicants, ranked and conflict-free for every open role at your company, instead of screening one job description at a time.
body:
## The problem

Screening was weeks of work that still produced the wrong matches. Over 150 candidates were read by hand every cycle. GPA cut-offs removed people who would have been good. And each role was filled on its own, one job description at a time, so every startup got a list built without reference to any other.

This was Challenge 2 — the CV matching bottleneck — one of three problems set at a 48-hour QSTP hackathon.

## What I built

Rubric makes the pool the product. Every resume goes into one open pool that never closes, and students keep adding to it between cycles.

A startup that needs one intern today gets the pool ranked for that role, with the reasons shown: a fit score, which of the role's core skills the candidate covers, and a signal for whether a human wrote the resume. Hidden gems surfaces the people a GPA cut-off had quietly rejected, and shows the evidence for each one.

Or the whole cycle runs in one pass. The allocation board spreads the pool across every startup at once, respects each one's capacity, and flags the contested picks — the candidates who rank top-three for more than one role. Any card can be dragged to override the result.

The assignment is greedy, and deliberately not an optimizer. It produces a defensible first pass that a human then adjusts, rather than an answer nobody can argue with.

## My role

I led Team Pantheon — three people, 48 hours, from the challenge brief to a working demo.

## Projected impact

The numbers below are projections, modelled from the challenge brief during the build. Rubric has not been run against a real intake, so none of this is measured.

- **4 hours** to place 900 applications across 6 roles in a single pass, against the two weeks of manual review the challenge described.
- **Zero** double-booked candidates per cycle, with every contested pick flagged before a human sees the list.

The plan for checking those claims was a post-cycle survey of the host startups plus the share of shortlisted students who reach interview. Neither has been run.

## Where it stands

A 48-hour prototype with a live demo. The screenshots use invented candidates, not real applicants.

Hidden gems, surfacing strong candidates that a GPA cut-off had rejected.
